title: Vibrational Sample-Based Quantum Diagonalization with Unitary-Cluster-Jastrow Ansätze on IBM QPUs
authors: Kunal Kumar, Erik Lötstedt, Yuri Kobayashi, Seiji Yunoki
abstract: We extend sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD) to anharmonic vibrational spectra and use it to benchmark how vibrational ansätze scale on present-day hardware under a direct one-hot encoding (up to 72 qubits). Five particle-conserving circuits are warm-started through vibrational coupled-cluster (VCC) t1, t2 amplitudes: UVCCSD, the compact heuristic circuit (CHC), and three unitary-cluster-Jastrow ansätze introduced here, VLUCJ, Vg-uCJ, and VIm-uCJ. A self-consistent configuration-recovery loop reconstructs correlated states from hardware samples in the low-retention regime where naïve post-selection breaks down, enabling the calculation of ground-state energies for H$_2$O, CH$_2$O, and CH$_2$ClF (3-9 modes). We compare harmonic-oscillator and vibrational self-consistent-field (VSCF, "modal") reference bases. In the small-modal-basis regime relevant for near-term devices, the modal basis is typically more accurate than the harmonic-oscillator representation; empirically, it also yields substantially better-converged hardware sampling for deep circuits at these qubit counts. Across ansätze, we find a clear retention/accuracy tradeoff when scaling: the new VLUCJ circuit is the most hardware-robust, retaining the largest fraction of physically valid one-hot outcomes, whereas the more expressive uCJ variants and UVCCSD can recover more correlation when retention is sufficient. Finally, we extend the recovery protocol to excited states by targeting a chosen per-mode VSCF occupation and warm-starting it with a state-specific VCC calculation, and we demonstrate the calculation of one representative fundamental vibrational frequency per molecule on IBM QPUs.
summary: This paper develops and tests advanced quantum algorithms for calculating the anharmonic vibrational spectra of molecules using quantum hardware. It compares several unitary-cluster-Jastrow ansätze, finding that hardware noise limits performance, but demonstrating that structured quantum sampling outperforms random guessing. The work successfully calculates fundamental vibrational frequencies on IBM QPUs, advancing the field's practical application to molecular physics.
main_problem: The paper addresses extending sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD) to accurately calculate anharmonic vibrational spectra of molecules using current quantum hardware.
main_result: The novel VLUCJ ansatz proved to be the most hardware-robust circuit structure, while the study successfully demonstrated calculating fundamental vibrational frequencies on IBM QPUs.
method: The authors employ SQD, warm-starting the process with vibrational coupled-cluster (VCC) amplitudes, and comparing multiple unitary-cluster-Jastrow ansätze on superconducting quantum processors.
model_or_system: The system models are the vibrational spectra of small molecules ($	ext{H}_2	ext{O}$, $	ext{CH}_2	ext{O}$, $	ext{CH}_2	ext{ClF}$), governed by a quartic force-field Hamiltonian derived from DFT calculations.
key_observables: Ground-state and excited-state energies, fundamental vibrational frequencies, and the fraction of physically valid one-hot outcomes (retention).
important_parameters: Qubit count up to 72, comparison between harmonic-oscillator and vibrational self-consistent-field (VSCF) reference bases, and the anharmonic coupling terms up to quartic order.
main_assumptions: The accuracy relies on the underlying potential energy surface approximation and the comparison highlights a trade-off between ansatz expressivity and hardware robustness.
figures_summary: Figures compare energy gaps and circuit performance (CZ count, depth) across different ansätze and sampling methods (random vs. structured quantum sample) on IBM hardware.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the theoretical framework (Hamiltonian, SQD), details the comparison of five ansätze, benchmarks performance on IBM QPUs by comparing results against random sampling and classical VSCF targets, and concludes with the calculation of representative vibrational frequencies.
why_interesting: This work directly tackles the application of quantum computation to molecular structure and dynamics, a core area of AMO physics, by benchmarking advanced quantum algorithms against real-world hardware noise.
